item.title: Your router's default IP range is sabotaging your WireGuard VPN
item.itunes:title: Your router's default IP range is sabotaging your WireGuard VPN
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
My WireGuard tunnel never actually dropped. The handshake stayed fresh, my NAS loaded, and yet my lab hostnames stopped resolving, ad blocking quietly switched off, and some services failed once before working on the second try. I'd already lost an evening to the Tailscale version of this problem, so I had a hunch about the cause.

The culprit is my home network's IP range. My eero hands out 192.168.4.0/22, the range my units shipped with, and any network I join that uses the same addresses can claim parts of my home network while I'm connected to it. I run a self-hosted VPN on Proxmox and filter everything through a high-availability Technitium DNS server, so I wanted proof, not theory. So I built a fake hotel network designed to collide with mine. What Windows did with it surprised me.

I run both Tailscale and WireGuard at home, and here's why you probably should too

Redundancy sounds like overkill until you actually need it.

9
By  Korbin Brown

I built a hotel network designed to collide with my home

A travel router, a cellular connection, and one very specific address

The stand-in hotel was a GL.iNet Mudi 7 running on Google Fi cellular, so every packet crossed the internet. I set its LAN to 192.168.4.61, which is exactly the address of my Technitium DNS server back home. That's mean, but it's also realistic, because a hotel router has to live somewhere, and the common ranges overlap constantly.

At home, a small Proxmox container holds a WireGuard server. The test laptop runs Windows 11 with WireGuard for Windows in split-tunnel mode, sending only 192.168.4.0/22 into the tunnel and using 192.168.4.61 for DNS. For every run, a PowerShell script captured the route table, the neighbor table, reachability, and DNS answers, so nothing below relies on my memory.

The VPN server fought me before the hotel did

Before any of that worked, my own router got in the way. The tunnel came up, ran for about three minutes, and then the server stopped receiving a single packet. A capture on the container showed zero inbound traffic on the WireGuard port, even though the port forward was still sitting in the eero app.

It turns out the eero only honors a port forward for a device it thinks is online, and a quiet container with a static IP gets marked offline fast. Switching the container to DHCP with a reservation helped, but the real fix was a ping every 20 seconds to keep it looking alive. If you self-host WireGuard behind an eero and it dies after a few minutes, check that first.

WGDashboard turns WireGuard's tedious setup into a 10-second QR code scan.

By  Dhruv Bhutani

Windows doesn't drop the tunnel, it hands out your addresses one at a time

Same-size ranges: the tunnel wins and the hotel loses

I expected the obvious failure, where the local network wins, and nothing reaches home. That's not what happened when both networks used the same /22. Windows had two routes for the exact same range, and when the prefix lengths tie, it picks the lower metric. The tunnel came in at an effective metric of 5 against 286 for Wi-Fi, so every home address went through WireGuard.

My NAS answered on port 5000, and Technitium handled DNS, exactly as if I were sitting at home. The cost lands on the hotel's side instead, because its own devices in that range are now unreachable from your laptop. That's fine until you need the hotel's captive portal.

A smaller hotel range wins, but only where something answers

Then I shrank the hotel network to a /24 sitting inside my /22. A more specific route always beats a broader one, so in theory every 192.168.4.x address should have gone to Wi-Fi and failed. Windows is a little cleverer than that. It tries Wi-Fi first, and when nothing answers the ARP request, it marks that neighbor unreachable and falls back to the tunnel.

The ping output caught it happening live. The first reply was "Destination host unreachable" from my own laptop, then two timeouts, then a reply from my Caddy server through the tunnel. So the first attempt fails and the retry works, which explains why this problem feels flaky rather than broken.

To prove it, I gave my iPhone a static IP of 192.168.4.64 on the travel router. Windows immediately sent Caddy's address to the phone instead; the TCP connection failed, and ping replies came back with a TTL of 64 instead of the 63 I got through the tunnel. My NAS at 192.168.7.69 kept working the whole time because the hotel network didn't cover it.

Changing your DNS doesn't hide anything, it just copies the list somewhere else

That doesn't mean you should keep using your ISP's DNS, however

3
By  Joe Rice-Jones

The quietest failure is DNS

My DNS server's address belonged to a travel router

Here's the catch with a hotel router. It's guaranteed to exist on its own network, and it usually sits on one of the most common addresses. In my test, it held 192.168.4.61, so every lookup aimed at my Technitium server went out over Wi-Fi to the travel router instead.

Public sites kept loading, so nothing looked wrong. But my lab hostnames came back empty, and a Grammarly telemetry domain that Technitium blocks resolved to real AWS addresses. Technitium's query log confirmed it: no queries arrived from the tunnel for those lookups. On a real network, whoever owns that address is answering your DNS, and you won't notice.

Why some apps keep resolving fine anyway

This is the part that makes the failure feel random. Both network adapters listed 192.168.4.61 as their DNS server, and Windows' own resolver appears to ask the lowest-metric adapter first, which is the tunnel. In the /24 runs, the system resolver still got Technitium's answer while a lookup aimed directly at the server got the travel router's.

When the tunnel was slow to respond, even the system resolver fell through to the hotel's answer. I didn't isolate that behavior on its own, but the captures line up with it. Apps that use the system resolver mostly keep working, and anything that talks to the DNS server directly quietly doesn't.

One DNS change fixed the "internet is slow" complaint I'd been chasing for months

Speed tests never caught it.

1
By  Samir Makwana

Fixes, from band-aid to cure

Pin the addresses that matter with /32 routes

The quick fix is adding host routes to AllowedIPs in the WireGuard config. A /32 is the most specific route, so it beats the hotel's /24 even when a real device is answering locally. I added 192.168.4.64/32 and 192.168.4.61/32 alongside /22, and with the phone still connected to the hotspot, Caddy came back through the tunnel, and Technitium was answering DNS again.

It works, but it only covers what you list, and the next hotel will collide with a different address. If you only pin one thing, make it your DNS server. The other option is NAT on the server, so remote clients see home as a fake range, which Tailscale's subnet routing handles natively with 4via6, but plain WireGuard makes you build it yourself.

Move home off the default range

The real cure is to avoid overlapping altogether. When I moved the travel router to 10.73.19.0/24, everything worked through the tunnel with no tricks, no /32 routes, and no retries. You can't renumber a hotel, though, so the network that has to move is yours.

Pick something odd in 10.0.0.0/8, like a random third octet, and avoid the router defaults everyone else uses: 192.168.0.x, 192.168.1.x, 10.0.0.x, and the 192.168.4.0/22 my eero units came with. Be especially careful about where your DNS server lands, because that's the address that got taken first.

Getting a public IP undid a year of CGNAT workarounds I'd built to survive it

CGNAT is gone. The setup isn't.

By  Shekhar Vaidya

Change it before you're sitting in a hotel lobby

The handshake looked healthy through every one of these tests. What failed was quieter: Windows handed my home addresses to the hotel network one at a time, starting with DNS, and only where something on that network answered. It's a lot harder to diagnose from a hotel room than a VPN that simply won't connect. If you're already on the road, compare your laptop's Wi-Fi address with your home range, and add a /32 for your DNS server if they overlap.

item.title: I added health checks to every Docker container, and now my homelab restarts its own broken services
item.itunes:title: I added health checks to every Docker container, and now my homelab restarts its own broken services
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
One morning, you wake up, open a service, only to find it inaccessible. And when you check your Docker containers or monitoring services, everything looks fine. I have faced it many times in the past, and most recently a few weeks ago with my Nextcloud service.

A tool auto-updated the Nextcloud container, but the database needed a manual migration. So, none of my monitoring services detected anything because the Docker container was up and running. That was when I decided to fix this by adding my own health check.

Why "running" doesn't mean "working"

Everything said "Up," but nothing worked.

I have been into homelabbing long enough to understand that if Docker says my container is up and running, that isn’t the final check. Docker doesn’t always know what’s happening inside the container; it only tracks the container’s lifecycle, whether the main process is alive.

I am not saying this from some theory I created myself or read somewhere. Similar things have happened to me more than once. I don’t exactly remember all the instances, but I can tell you about a recent one.

A few weeks ago, I was testing Watchtower. It was a service to automate Docker container image updates. On paper, it looked good; it removed the boring task of updating each container. I deployed it and let it run for a few days. Everything was good; it was updating all the containers. But one morning I opened my Nextcloud service in the browser and found a database error.

What happened was Watchtower pulled a new image, and that image’s code was ahead of the database schema, which threw a schema-breaking version error. The fix was easy: I ran docker exec nextcloud php occ upgrade, and it was done. But the fix isn’t the story. There was an issue with the service, but since Docker showed it up and running, my monitoring service didn’t catch it.

The point is the container was up, but the application was broken. I recreated the failure with a two-minute test. I started by creating a throwaway Nginx container and breaking the app from inside, but not the container. The curl command showed it as broken, but docker ps showed it as up and running. This is something you can test yourself.

docker run -d --name up-but-dead -p 18081:80 nginx
curl -I localhost:18081
docker exec up-but-dead sh -c 'rm /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf && nginx -s reload'
curl -I localhost:18081; docker ps --filter name=up-but-dead

So, should Docker’s default monitoring be enough? In my case, I added another layer to check the health of the service, not just the container.

5 Docker Compose tricks that made my home server more reliable

A collection of tips and tricks that leveled up my Docker Compose game

By  Ayush Pande

item.title: I unlocked RTX 50-series features on my RTX 4070 Ti, and Nvidia's GPU generations don't make sense anymore
item.itunes:title: I unlocked RTX 50-series features on my RTX 4070 Ti, and Nvidia's GPU generations don't make sense anymore
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When I bought my RTX 4070 Ti GPU in 2023, it was pretty much the third-best card I could buy from Nvidia. The one thing I was absolutely fawning over was the possibility of frame generation with the new GPU, which, at the time, was an exclusive feature for RTX 40 series GPUs.

Fast-forward to 2026, and RTX 50 series cards are now a year old, and they support all the way up to 6x Frame Generation — boasting frame rate numbers I couldn't possibly replicate on my GPU. Then came other features exclusive to the new Blackwell architecture, and it was tough not to be envious of the new cards running Reflex 2, and, of course, DLSS 5.

Over the past month, however, I've installed and used each one of these "exclusive" features on my RTX 4070 Ti, and the results have been considerably more interesting than I anticipated. Sure, some work better than others, but the implications are difficult to ignore.

DLSS 4.5 is expensive, but it’s the best thing to happen to my aging RTX PC

The upside is remarkable, but the cost isn't equal for all.

19
By  Samarveer Singh

Multi Frame Generation works on my RTX 4070 Ti

Nvidia’s 6x MFG now has a larger "exclusive" club

After 2x Frame Generation became all the rage with the RTX 40 series, it still took a while for the technology to become polished and reach its near-flawless quality that it boasts today. Then came Multi Frame Generation on the RTX 50 series, thanks to more Tensor cores on the new Blackwell architecture. Naturally, my RTX 4070 Ti was not invited to the party.

OptiScaler, however, changed that. Using the appropriate DLSS DLLs and OptiScaler's features that support frame generation even on titles and cards that aren't built for it at all, I had MFG running on my RTX 4070 Ti in no time. In fact, while playing The Blood of Dawnwalker, I went from 96 fps on 2x Frame Generation to 160 fps on 4x Frame Generation on 4K High settings.

Moreover, the image quality remained astoundingly clear and crisp even with 4x Frame Generation running on an "unsupported" card. The reason I couldn't test 5x and 6x Frame Generation was simply because I ran out of VRAM on my 12GB GPU.

Frame Generation requires 1–2 GB extra VRAM on supported cards. Moving to higher multipliers like 4x, 5x, or 6x Frame Generation adds a minor 300–350 MB overhead per multiplier.

I found the perfect sweet spot at 3x Frame Generation using OptiScaler in my games, which is still one major step above the 2x multiplier my card was officially destined to stay stuck with. My RTX 4070 Ti may not have magically become a Blackwell GPU overnight, but it definitely crossed a software boundary that Nvidia presented as a generational one.

3 reasons gamers prefer upscaling over frame generation

Gamers don't consider frame generation all that hot, but happily use upscaling to boost frames

18
By  Tanveer Singh

DLSS 5, too, is running on my RTX 4070 Ti

Nvidia's neural rendering tech isn't confined to Blackwell anymore

After using MFG on my RTX 40-series card, DLSS 5 blurred the line even further between the two generations of GPUs. Nvidia designed its latest neural rendering tech around its newest GPUs, but I've spent the past couple of weeks running DLSS 5 on my card across a plethora of games. Neither the card nor the games I've been "remastering" using DLSS 5, are supposed to run it, and yet, they do. At this point, I'm almost getting used to seeing "RTX 50-series exclusive" followed by "but it works on my 4070 Ti."

Nvidia has stated that DLSS 5 support will soon reach RTX 40-series GPUs as well.

The setup is surprisingly accessible. OptiScaler, ReShade and the relevant neural-rendering components can inject DLSS 5 into games that don’t officially support it. Of course, if you want a one-click DLSS 5 injection, you can always use tools and utilities like DLSS 5 Swapper and DLSS 5 Manager, which make the whole process considerably less painful. I myself have used DLSS 5's neural rendering with PCSX2 and RPCS3 to play my favorite PlayStation 2 and PlayStation 3 games and experience them in a new light.

Unless you've been living under a rock, you already know that DLSS 5 is absolutely hammering even the strongest RTX 50-series cards. Even the RTX 5090 loses half its frame rate with DLSS 5 turned on. Naturally, my RTX 4070 Ti suffered a larger performance penalty, but with other features like Smooth Motion and moving the neural renderer's place in the pipeline, I've achieved a more-than-playable frame rate in each game I used DLSS 5. My 4070 Ti still has the same hardware it shipped with, but OptiScaler let me try something Nvidia never intended it to do.

We have reached the GPU ceiling, and AI tricks like DLSS are how companies pretend we haven't

Silicon alone can only do so much without software bearing the load

14
By  Samarveer Singh

Reflex 2 is also creeping onto RTX 40-series GPUs

RTX 40-series support is coming, but it's delayed

Reflex 2 is another RTX 50-series feature that Nvidia has tied to its latest generation. This feature in particular is rather interesting, since Frame Warp needs access to the rendered frame at a very specific point in the pipeline. Of course, as is par for the course, the PC modding community has found ways to bring that technology to older hardware, albeit in parts.

Instead of generating an entirely new frame, Frame Warp in Reflex 2 takes an already rendered frame and adjusts it using the latest input information. This allows the displayed image to better reflect what the player just did on their controller, keyboard, or mouse. That's how Reflex 2 dissipates the perceived latency, and it never even asks the GPU to render an entirely new frame.

As of October 2026, Nvidia's Reflex 2 with Frame Warp is still pending for RTX 40-series GPUs, although modders claim to have run it on even older RTX GPUs.

As always, the usual community implementations can't magically add any missing Blackwell silicon to older GPUs, but they can still hook into this process through software. This doesn't give me something identical to native Reflex 2 support, thanks to the obvious compatibility and implementation limitations. And yet, at the end of the day, it's still more performance than I had on day one.

Clearly, some of what we call "generation-exclusive" is software sitting on top of hardware that can already do more than Nvidia's official feature matrix may suggest.

Your GPU's upscaler has a secret second job, and nobody's talking about it

Upscaling doesn't just boost your frame rate

1
By  Samarveer Singh

My RTX 4070 Ti is closer to an RTX 5070 than ever before

Software is softening the walls between GPU generations

Full disclosure: no matter how many hoops I jump through to run Blackwell-only features on my Ada Lovelace card, software can never manufacture hardware. My RTX 4070 Ti still has the same 12GB of VRAM, its existing CUDA and Tensor cores, and the same architecture it had on the assembly line. If a feature genuinely depends on newer hardware, an RTX 40-series card isn't going to sprout those capabilities overnight.

When it comes to GPU generations, hardware still defines the ceiling, but software increasingly defines the parts of the ceiling you're allowed to reach.

But that isn't where things get interesting. MFG, DLSS 5, and parts of Reflex 2 show that some features we increasingly associate with a GPU generation can exist as software layers that interact with hardware an older GPU already possesses. Once those layers become accessible, the generational boundary gets surprisingly fuzzy. I even deleted an RTX 5070 Ti that I've had in my Amazon cart for a full year now after I got Multi Frame Generation working on my card.

Consequently, this genuinely changes how I think about GPU generations. Hardware still defines the ceiling, but software increasingly defines exactly which parts of that ceiling you're allowed to reach. Nvidia can draw the line wherever it wants on an official compatibility chart. The PC modding community has repeatedly demonstrated that the line itself can be considered more permeable than it looks.

DLSS 5 Manager
See at Github
I pushed FSR 4.1 and DLSS 4.5 to their limits on older hardware, and one changed my mind about 4K gaming

It was neck-and-neck, until it wasn't

6
By  Samarveer Singh

The GPU generation I bought isn't quite the GPU generation I have anymore

As someone who only ever looked forward to their next GPU after a few years of use, it's been genuinely strange to see my RTX 4070 Ti keep finding new tricks. I bought the GPU as a piece of hardware with a very specific set of capabilities, and yet, the software ecosystem around it keeps expanding what that definition means. Despite remaining the same card I installed on my motherboard in 2023, it has gained new possibilities.

We used to think of a GPU generation as a hard boundary, where new features only came with a new card. Now, however, I'm not so sure. That hardware still matters enormously, of course, but the software sitting between that hardware and the games we play is becoming just as important.

item.title: I stopped looking for a free video editor after finding one that handles keyframing like Adobe and CapCut (and it's only two months old)
item.itunes:title: I stopped looking for a free video editor after finding one that handles keyframing like Adobe and CapCut (and it's only two months old)
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Not paying for editing software seems like the more convenient route, but that's not always the case. Sure, you don't have a bill to deal with, but you usually have to put up with the quirks and shortcomings of free editors. The easy ones let you handle the basics, but as soon as you want to animate a bit of text you're out of options. While the more complex ones either chew resources or are just hard to navigate. It's not easy finding something that sits in the middle.

Drift turned up in my search for new editors, and it sits perfectly in that balanced middle. It's a free, open-source editor from CutWire Studios, a nonprofit, and its first public release only went out at the end of July, but it's already on version 0.7. It even has an AI agent built in, but I left that out for my first test run because that deserves its own moment, and I wanted to see how it holds up without the AI.

This open-source tool combines Photoshop, Premiere Pro, and After Effects - And it replaced all three for me

I didn't expect it to replace my entire Adobe setup

13
By  Nolen Jonker

Drift gives you everyday editing without the learning curve

If you've used any editor before, you'll already know this one

If you know your way around video editors, then you already know how to navigate all of Drift's basics. It uses a proper multi-track timeline, and the select and blade tools sit on V and B the same as CapCut, so my hands just went to the right keys.

I like its reframing feature. You drag a box over the part of the shot you want, and Drift saves that framing while the original video stays available, so you can come back later and frame it differently. I tried it on some landscape stock footage for a vertical cut, and being able to nudge the frame around afterwards was better than defaulting to cropping.

The quickest way to make anything move on the screen is through its presets. Every clip gets its own in and out animation, set separately, so a clip can slide in from the right and then just fade away at the end, or not animate out at all. And there's also a big range of text styles so you're not building every title from scratch, and you get a bunch of adjustable properties like outline and glow.

Combined with the other basic tools like cutting and trimming, this is pretty much all you need for basic edits for a social media account. Anything I styled myself could be saved and reused, and the effects browser previews every effect on a frame from your actual clip, which saves a lot of applying and undoing.

The free video editor I use instead of Premiere hasn't asked me for a subscription in five years

It's completely free, but that's not why I stayed

By  Nolen Jonker

You can keyframe almost anything

With a full graph editor

Keyframing is where Drift starts getting a little more serious. Nearly every value in the properties panel has a small diamond next to it that sets a keyframe at the playhead, even the audio and settings inside effects. With Auto keyframes switched on you don't even need the diamond, because changing a value with the playhead parked records one for you.

Each property has its own easing options too, so for example Ease accelerates out and decelerates in. And then there's also a full graph editor you can expand from the top of the timeline. I always like customizing my Bezier curves with the little handles, that's just the quintessential Adobe experience I learned to keyframe with, so having this in a free editor is always nice to have.

The graph is a tad clunky. Although I do like being able to adjust its size, I think because of its position, some might miss that they're able to extend it, and therefore won't have enough real estate for custom keyframing.

Stabilization uses the same system. Instead of baking a fix into the clip, it writes position keyframes, so the result shows up on that graph where you can tweak it, and there's a tripod mode for locking a shot down entirely. These advanced features are usually pretty rare to find in a completely free editor.

I replaced Premiere Pro with a free video editor, and I haven't missed the subscription once

A free NLE with Hollywood credits

1
By  Nolen Jonker

Audio isn't an afterthought

It goes beyond just a volume slider

Audio tends to be where free editors lose me because it usually just consists of a volume slider and maybe some fade ins/outs. Drift shows clip volume in decibels, which already lets me know they're a little more serious about audio control. And you can also keyframe every audio component just like you can the visual stuff.

The effect chain has more to it. There's a proper compressor with real threshold and ratio controls (attack and release too), sitting next to EQ and a voice leveler in a utility category that's clearly aimed at cleaning up dialogue. Further down the list there are novelty filters like telephone and underwater. The latest release also added a mixer with per-track strips and stereo meters. Ultimately, the audio of your clips doesn't have to get neglected here.

A library of assets

Take your pick

In the Market tab, there's a library called Drift Assets, made up of animated graphics CutWire makes specifically for Drift. They're Lottie animations, so they scale cleanly, and you can recolor them too. Adding one at the playhead drops it onto its own graphic track.

I recommend reading the license before using any of them though. Drift Assets are under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, which means crediting Drift Assets wherever they appear and not using them for anything commercial, and if you adapt one, your version goes out under that same license, so I'd probably keep them off a monetized channel. The Stock tab is a separate thing that browses outside sources, and it asks you to accept terms before loading.

This video editor does 90% of what Premiere does for free

Paying for a video editor doesn’t necessarily mean you get more out of it

6
By  Nolen Jonker

Early software that's surprisingly deep

Two months in and Drift already has a mature keyframe editor, audio control, and a stabilizer that hands you its own keyframes to edit, which is pretty impressive. There are a few rough spots, but compared to some of the open-source editors I've been using for years, it's genuinely modern and easy to navigate. CutWire pushes updates often, so we can probably expect the feature set to grow pretty quickly.

CutWire Drift
See at CutWire Drift

item.title: I stopped clearing Windows caches after discovering it was silently costing me performance
item.itunes:title: I stopped clearing Windows caches after discovering it was silently costing me performance
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Every once in a while, a Windows 11 optimization guide will tell you to "clear your cache" to reclaim some storage space on your SSD or speed up your PC. It's probably one of the most repeated maintenance tip that gets passed around on tech forums as well.

Most of the time, it's generally harmless, but depending on what you clear, you could be gaining just a few hundred megabytes of storage in exchange for long loading times and additionally making Windows and apps redo the work they have already done.

As with anything, there's a time and place for clearing caches, and that time is when your drive is running low on space or if something has gone wrong. Treating this method as routine maintenance can often be counterintuitive, though. Here's what the three most popular cleanup options remove, and what you sacrifice to get some space back.

The Settings cleanup is harmless, unless you tick two boxes

Thumbnail and shader cache aren't junk, whatever the list calls them

Perhaps the most popular way to clear cache on Windows 11 that most users will be familiar with is Settings > System > Storage > Temporary files. Through the Settings app, Windows gives you a list of things it considers "safe" to remove, but the problem with this familiar approach is that the list mixes leftovers with caches that your PC routinely requires.

Anything related to Delivery Optimization is fine to clear. These are the files that Windows downloads as a part of its update delivery system and stores temporarily so that updates can be shared with other PCs on your local network or the internet. Windows already manages this cache itself, sets a default cache expiration date (which is exactly 3 days) and the default maximum cache size is 20% of disk capacity.

The two that I prefer to leave alone are Thumbnails and DirectX Shader Cache. Windows Explorer uses its thumbnail cache to avoid rebuilding image and video previews every time you revisit a folder, while the Windows DirectX shader cache stores graphics work your games have already done. If you empty either, Windows and applications will simply start rebuilding it from scratch, and function slower than usual.

That being said, there are some special circumstances that warrant clearing the shader cache and thumbnail cache. For example, Epic Games recommends clearing the Nvidia DXCache (and the equivalent AMD DxCache on AMD systems) when titles like Fortnite deliver below the expected performance or if excessive stuttering is observed on DirectX12. It is worth noting that these are separate from the Windows DirectX Shader Cache entry.

You can also keep an eye on the size of the DXCache size through a utility called WizTree, which is how I discovered an Nvidia setting had allowed it to balloon up to 40GB, which is a rather disproportionate amount of storage for a cache whose job is to make games load and run more smoothly.

Similarly, a user might want to clear the thumbnail cache for a slightly different reason. Windows can retain thumbnail data even after the original files have been deleted, which can matter if you keep sensitive photos or use a shared PC. Outside these specific use cases though, there isn't much performance or storage to be reclaimed clearing these, and doing so only makes your PC work harder to rebuild them over time.

5 reasons you should avoid PC cleaning apps and use Windows Disk Cleanup instead

They're more trouble than they're worth

10
By  João Carrasqueira

Clearing Prefetch can make your app launches slower

It looks disposable, but Windows and your apps have a use for it

Windows introduced Prefetch in its Windows XP era, and it continues to persist on modern Windows 11 systems. What it does is basically record which files and resources an application requires during startup so that the OS can preload them more efficiently on every subsequent launch.

The common advice is to open C:\Windows\Prefetch and delete everything inside it to boost your system's performance. There's very little to gain from doing this, though. Not only is it redundant (Windows simply recreates the files as you launch those applications again), your frequently launched apps will be measurably slower upon startup, which hits your workflow where it hurts the most.

There are legitimate reasons to clear Prefetch, though, but as with the rest of the items I've listed, most of them involve troubleshooting specific Windows problems. As far as storage is concerned, there really isn't much to reclaim considering the size of the Prefetch folder on the average PC.

Manually emptying the Temp folder by hand skips a check Windows runs

It's not always wise to clear %temp%

One of the quickest ways to clear temporary files is to hit Windows + R, type in %temp%, and then select all and delete everything you find. On certain systems, it'll clear the most junk out of any other approach, but it also happens to be the bluntest in what it does.

Disk Cleanup (and Storage Sense) both deliberately skip temporary files that have been modified within the last seven days, and they do so because it's a built-in safety rule. Manually selecting and deleting everything in the %temp% folder, as you'd expect, ignores that filter entirely.

Microsoft's description of these temporary files says that programs usually clean up after themselves when they close, and anything that's left untouched for more than a week is generally safe to remove. Manual intervention here throws the seven-day rule out of the window. Deletion of some files may be blocked by an in-use error, but that's applied only to the files that are in use at the time when the action is performed.

The cost of this error is small, but nonetheless, noticeable. Microsoft's .NET documentation notes that single-file apps that use extraction unpack themselves into a .net folder inside the Temp directory before they run, so clearing it means they have to unpack all over again on the next launch.

8 ways you are unknowingly ruining your Windows experience

Windows habits that are secretly killing PC performance

4
By  Parth Shah

Not every cache file is junk

What most guides on the subject tend to forget (or omit) is the fact that caches exist because a process was slow the first time, and clearing it makes it slow all over again. That being said, there's merit in clearing cache files in certain specific situations, such as when an app is throwing errors, facing performance issues, or if a cache file is bloating beyond its usual size.

The key mistake that one should be mindful of is treating every cache file as junk. Likewise, deleting every cache file doesn't yield a measurable performance uplift or free up storage, and can often be counterproductive in practice.

item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Productivity software has changed a lot over the years. Every few months, there seems to be a new app promising to organize my work, save time, or completely change how I get things done. I’ve tried plenty of those tools myself, and some have genuinely been useful. But I’ve also noticed that a few much older apps keep surviving every new wave. They may not have flashy interfaces or the latest features, but they continue to earn a spot on my PC. After using them for years, I’ve realized there is something valuable about software that simply stays useful without constantly trying to reinvent itself.

Everything

Fastest way to find files

Everything is one of those Windows apps I installed years ago and never really had a reason to remove. I often keep it open in the background because it makes finding files feel almost instant. Instead of digging through folders or remembering exactly where I saved something, I can start typing the filename and get to it quickly.

What I like most is how predictable it feels. I don't have to change how I work just because I'm using it. I type what I'm looking for, scan the results, and open the file. That's it.

I’ve used it for everything from tracking down old documents to finding files buried several folders deep. It has become one of those small utilities I barely think about until I have to use a computer without it. Then I immediately notice it's missing.

Everything
Individual pricing
Free
Platforms
Windows

Everything indexes all the files on your computer within seconds, and you can find any file or folder you are looking for quickly.

See at VoidTools

7-Zip

My go-to tool for archives

7-Zip is another old-school app that has quietly stayed on my computer for years. I use it whenever I need to package a group of files together or open an archive someone has sent me. It handles the job without making me think about which app should open the file or whether I need another tool installed.

I especially like how it fits naturally into File Explorer. I can right-click a file or folder, choose the 7-Zip option, and get the task done without opening a separate application first. It feels like a utility that belongs in Windows rather than something I have to actively manage.

There are plenty of newer archive tools around, but I rarely feel the need to look for alternatives. 7-Zip has been reliable enough that I simply keep using it whenever I need it.

7-Zip

7-Zip is the best and most powerful replacement for paid archiving software.

See at 7-Zip

Ditto

The old-school clipboard tool I trust

My clipboard used to be one of those small things that constantly interrupted my workflow. I would copy something, copy something else, and then realize I needed the previous item again. That changed once I started using Ditto.

I use it when writing, researching, and moving information between different apps. I can copy several pieces of text one after another and come back to them whenever I need. It is especially useful when I am collecting information from different sources and don't want to keep switching between windows.

What makes it stick around is how naturally it fits into my workflow. I don't need to plan around it or change how I work. I simply copy things as usual and use the clipboard history whenever I need something I copied earlier. It solves a small problem that comes up surprisingly often.

Ditto

Ditto is a simple clipboard manager for Windows that adds a lot more functionality, including the ability to remember copied files and retain items indefinitely.

item.title: Hints of the Steam Deck 2 begin to emerge as a leak reveals a mysterious "Gainsborough" APU
item.itunes:title: Hints of the Steam Deck 2 begin to emerge as a leak reveals a mysterious "Gainsborough" APU
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • AMD driver leak references 'Gainsborough' APU—strong hint a Steam Deck 2 is in the works.
  • Codename nod to 'Aerith'—Gainsborough is her surname, implying a direct sequel APU for the Deck.
  • Gainsborough likely N3P semi-custom chip for handhelds; Valve wants a generational leap—still unconfirmed.

With the Steam Machine, Steam Frame, and the new Steam Controller now available to purchase or preorder, there's a weird hole in Valve's hardware releases: where on earth is the Steam Deck 2? While the company hasn't confirmed or denied its existence, a recent leak points to a good possibility that one is currently in the works.

AMD's "Gainsborough" APU hints at a potential Steam Deck 2 release

Nothing has been confirmed, though

As reported on the YouTube channel Moore's Law is Dead, something interesting is happening with AMD APUs. Tucked away within the AMD drivers are references to something called "Gainsborough." While that's usually noteworthy in and of itself, mounting circumstantial evidence suggests "Gainsborough" will power the Steam Deck 2.

For instance, there's the codename. The original Steam Deck's APU used the codename "Aerith" from the classic RPG Final Fantasy VII. "Gainsborough" is her surname, so a new APU that uses the second half of her full name is pretty likely.

Next, Gainsborough seems to be equipped to handle TSMC's N3P node. This is one of the most efficient 3-nanometer variants available, and it would make complete sense if Gainsborough was destined to be used in handheld consoles—like the Steam Deck 2, for example.

Finally, it seems AMD designed Gainsborough as a semi-custom chip, rather than something that gets shipped to laptop and handheld manufacturers for general use. Moore's Law is Dead spoke with some of their insiders in the AMD OED scene, and none of them had heard of Gainsborough, which strongly hints that the APU will find itself in a specific product.

Valve isn't ditching Windows or x86, but it's quietly making both optional

Valve wants to make it possible for gamers to play anywhere.

3
By  Adam Conway

The timeline lines up with a Steam Deck 2 release

Things are looking likely for a new console

Alright, so how likely is it that this is evidence that the Steam Deck 2 is in production? Well, from what we can tell from outside of Valve's HQ, the chances of it working on a new Steam Deck are pretty high. Lawrence Yang of Valve confirmed two years ago that Valve was interested in making a Steam Deck 2, but it didn't want to simply release a console with marginally higher specs, as it would be unfair to its consumers:

​​​​​​​"So, we really do want to wait for a generational leap in compute without sacrificing battery life before we ship the real second generation of Steam Deck. But it is something that we're excited about and we're working on."

Moore's Law is Dead speculated that a Steam Deck 2 based on this hardware would be akin to upgrading an Xbox One to an Xbox Series X or a PlayStation 5, which would likely be a strong enough reason to convince Valve to release a new handheld console. Alas, as is the norm with these leaks, nothing has been outright stated and should be taken with a grain of salt until confirmed otherwise.

Someone squeezed the Steam Deck's hardware into a custom Game Boy shell, and it looks amazing

Hey Valve, maybe take some notes from this one.

By  Simon Batt

item.title: I changed my Fire TV Stick’s DNS to unlock more content, but it fixed something even more annoying
item.itunes:title: I changed my Fire TV Stick’s DNS to unlock more content, but it fixed something even more annoying
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
In the past, I have often managed to bypass geo-blocking and other restrictions by switching DNS servers. It's the most feasible option, since a VPN generally slows down your connection. So, I tried the same with my Fire TV Stick, and to my surprise, it fixed a much bigger problem, something that I wasn't even actively focused on.

For those who are unaware, DNS or Domain Name System, often called the internet's phone book, is simply put, a database. While we use domain names like "xda-developers.com" to access websites, machines use IP addresses. And this is where DNS comes into the picture. It translates human-readable domain names into machine-readable IP addresses. The problem is that the default DNS on routers and devices isn't always the best for performance, and switching to another DNS server can do wonders.

It improved connectivity

Faster loading and less buffering

As surprising as it may sound, changing your Fire TV Stick's DNS, or even the one on your smart TV, improves connectivity and minimizes related issues. Also, content loads faster and buffers less, as long as you're on a decent internet plan. If the internet speed itself is slow, switching DNS won't do much good.

Let's understand how switching DNS can help with streaming. A better-performing DNS connects your Fire TV Stick to a better server, improving load times. This difference in performance becomes noticeable if the default DNS is slow, overloaded, or directing you to a less-than-optimal server. For my Fire TV Stick, I picked Cloudflare's DNS since it's one of the most reliable, at least as far as I know. Google's public DNS is good too, and I would have tried it next had Cloudflare's DNS not performed well. But it didn't come down to that. Maybe I will try Google's in a week or so.

Keep in mind that you can also change the router's DNS. Since I was simply trying to bypass content restrictions on the Fire TV Stick, I didn't want to reconfigure things at the network level. But that should work too, if you are more comfortable with that.

6 useful Fire TV Stick apps that really improve my streaming experience

Stop scrolling, start streaming.

3
By  Parth Shah

Changing DNS on Fire TV Stick is simple

It takes about two minutes

You can easily change the DNS on your Fire TV Stick. It's not as straightforward as switching DNS on a PC, but it's pretty simple. First, open Settings on your Fire TV Stick, go to Device and Software, then into About, and scroll down to Network. You should now see the IP address, Gateway, and current DNS on the right. Take a picture of this, as we'll need this information in a minute.

Now, go back to Settings, then into Network, select the connected network, and choose Forget this network. Then reselect the network from the list, enter the password, and select "Advanced" at the bottom. It will now ask you for the IP address. Enter what you captured in the picture earlier. Similarly, fill out the Gateway field. For Network Prefix Length, enter the number currently shown in the field, then proceed. You will now be asked for the DNS details. Since we are using Cloudflare's DNS, enter 1.1.1.1 under DNS 1 and 1.0.0.1 under DNS 2. That's it. Your Fire TV Stick now has a new DNS.

To confirm everything is in order, do a quick reboot, then check whether the new DNS holds. For most of you, it should. But it is still worth checking.

It won't unlock more content
